edges.description: Failure of distal proton secretion reduces net acid excretion.
Failed distal acidification is the clinical dRTA phenotype.
Retained acid produces systemic hyperchloremic acidosis.
Inappropriately alkaline urine is a direct readout of failed distal acidification.
Reduced ammonium excretion is read out as a positive urine anion gap.
Chloride is retained with the normal-anion-gap acidosis.
The acidosis and distal transport derangement drive urinary potassium loss.
Chronic acidosis raises urinary calcium and lowers urinary citrate.
Sustained acidosis is the upstream cause of the mineral and calcitriol disturbance producing the skeletal disease.
intermediate_mechanisms: sustained systemic metabolic acidosis with urinary calcium loss and secondary calcitriol deficiency

edges.description: Urinary potassium loss lowers serum potassium.
The node is read out clinically as hypercalciuria.

nodes.description: A combination controlled-release potassium bicarbonate and potassium citrate preparation approved in Europe. nodes.description: Chronic uncorrected metabolic acidosis places dRTA on the calciopenic arm of the defective skeletal mineralization module. Urinary calcium loss reduces the calcium reaching the mineralization front, and net renal generation of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D falls even though 25-hydroxyvitamin D supply is intact. That the limiting step is the acidosis is what alkali therapy demonstrates: correcting the acidosis alone raises serum calcitriol and heals the bone disease.

evidence.reference_title: Distal renal tubular acidosis: alkali heals osteomalacia and increases net production of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
evidence.snippet: In 2 women with distal renal tubular acidosis and osteomalacia, alkali treatment cured the bone disease and was accompanied by marked increases in the serum 1,25 dihydroxyvitamin D concentration, without a significant change in the 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration.

nodes.description: A knockin mouse carrying the murine equivalent of the most common human dominant dRTA variant R589H. It reproduces an incomplete dRTA and the intercalated-cell loss seen in human disease while, notably, the mutant protein is still targeted basolaterally - so the in vivo phenotype is driven by intercalated-cell depletion and V-ATPase mistargeting rather than simple basolateral mislocalisation.
Inappropriately alkaline urine (pH > 5.5) despite systemic acidosis; a direct readout of the distal acidification failure.

nodes.description: The disease-specific supersaturation trigger of the nephrolithiasis module: in dRTA the lithogenic combination is persistently alkaline urine (which favours calcium phosphate) together with hypercalciuria and the loss of citrate, the normal inhibitor of calcium crystallisation. This raises urinary supersaturation with respect to calcium phosphate and drives crystal nucleation, producing nephrocalcinosis and nephrolithiasis - the latter disproportionately frequent in SLC4A1 disease.

nodes.description: A heterozygous pathogenic SLC4A1 variant produces a mutant kidney anion exchanger 1 (kAE1). The dominant alleles cluster at the Arg589 hotspot and at other transmembrane or C-terminal residues (Ser613Phe, Gly609Arg, the Arg901X truncation, Met909Thr). Importantly, the mutant protein usually retains much of its intrinsic chloride/bicarbonate exchange activity - the defect is where the protein goes, not whether it can transport.

nodes.description: Lifelong oral alkali - sodium bicarbonate and/or potassium citrate, with additional potassium chloride as needed - corrects the systemic acidosis and hypokalemia. Potassium citrate does double duty, since urinary citrate is the inhibitor of calcium precipitation depleted in this disease. It replaces the buffer the kidney cannot regenerate; it does not repair the kAE1 defect, and the urine stays inappropriately alkaline.
